title: Nepal, China Warn of Fresh Flood Risks as Barrier Lakes Threaten to Burst
excerpt: Two debris-dammed lakes on either side of the border risk collapse as nearly 1,000 people remain missing from this week's catastrophic glacier flood.
body:
• Nepal and China warned Thursday of fresh flooding risks as two debris-dammed lakes on either side of their border threaten to burst, days after a catastrophic glacier collapse killed at least 362 people.
  • China said 3 million cubic meters of water are expected to flow into an already dammed lake over the next three days, with peak flow expected around September 1.
  • Nearly 1,000 people remain missing, including 288 Indian nationals in Nepal and another 200 stranded in China, along with hundreds of other foreign tourists and pilgrims.
  • Rescue workers began moving to higher ground after Nepal's disaster authority issued an urgent warning about the rising lake at the flood site.

Nepal and China issued urgent warnings Thursday of fresh flood risks in the Himalayas as two lakes formed by debris from this week's catastrophic glacier collapse threaten to burst, raising the prospect of a secondary disaster in a region where rescuers are still searching for nearly 1,000 missing people.

The warnings came two days after a massive glacier collapse sent a wall of rock, ice, mud, and debris cascading through Himalayan river systems, devastating villages and key infrastructure along the Nepal-China border route that connects Kathmandu with Lhasa in Tibet — a corridor heavily used by trekkers and pilgrims.

Two Lakes, Two Warnings

Nepal's disaster management authority warned that a lake formed by debris blocking the Bhotekoshi River at the flood site is rising and at risk of bursting, urging residents, travelers, and rescue workers to move away from riverbanks.

"The volume of water is continuing to increase, and so is the risk."

— Zhu Jinfeng, Researcher, China Water Resources Ministry

On the Chinese side, authorities warned that 3 million cubic meters of water — roughly equivalent to 1,200 Olympic-sized swimming pools — are expected to flow into an already dammed lake over the next three days, creating a high risk of a breach. Peak flow is expected around September 1.

Aerial footage captured by a Chinese rescue team showed masses of brown water accumulating in a basin with no visible outlet, with water already submerging bushes and trees and pushing against a barrier of debris and stones, state broadcaster CGTN reported.

Rescue Operations Under Threat

The warnings forced some rescue teams to halt their work and retreat to higher ground. Pawan Koirala, leading a 13-member rescue team in Nepal, said his group began moving away from the riverbed after the alert was issued.

"We are here for rescue and don't want to be near the danger zone," Koirala told Reuters.

Rainfall forecast over the coming week is expected to worsen the threat, Chinese state media reported, citing the country's water resources ministry. On the Chinese side, light to moderate rainfall has already loosened soil and rock around the precarious zone upstream.

Massive International Search Continues

At least 362 people have been confirmed dead across Nepal and China's Tibet, with nearly 1,000 still missing — more than half of them foreigners from over two dozen countries. The missing foreigners in Nepal include 288 from India, 63 from the United States, 53 from Ukraine, 51 from Malaysia, 35 from Australia, 33 from the United Kingdom, and 25 from Canada.

In China's Tibet, the tally of missing in Gyirong county reached 558, including 260 foreigners, according to state broadcaster CCTV. Chinese rescuers had yet to reach the worst-hit area by Thursday evening, as crews worked to clear debris from the key access road.

India's foreign ministry said it was coordinating with Nepal to assist its nationals affected by the floods. The Indian embassy in Kathmandu and authorities in several states, including Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Andhra Pradesh, have set up helplines for families seeking information. Many of the missing Indians were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a site in Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists.

What Comes Next

Chinese authorities have mobilized an engineering team to conduct aerial surveys and 3D modeling of the barrier lake. The general approach is to excavate a drainage channel to relieve pressure, but engineers said calculations on water flow and fill rates are still underway. Weather monitoring over the coming days will be critical as continued rainfall could accelerate the crisis.
